---
title: "Tutorial: the deforming Earth"
subtitle: "A conceptual tour of the physics and numerics behind VILMA2"
---

VILMA2 computes how the solid Earth and sea level respond to a changing load of
ice and ocean water. This page introduces the ideas behind the model, one at a
time, for a reader who is new to glacial isostatic adjustment (GIA) or to this
code. Each section gives the physical idea, its central equation and a short
note on where it lives in VILMA2. The detailed derivations, parameters and
validation are on the linked pages. The page assumes some familiarity with
linear algebra and partial differential equations, and nothing about the code.

## Refreshers and name origins

Two mathematical ideas recur throughout the model. The first is
**diagonalization**. A linear operator $L$ is diagonal in a basis of its
eigenfunctions $\phi_k$, since $L\phi_k = \lambda_k\phi_k$. A field expanded in
that basis, $f = \sum_k c_k\phi_k$, then transforms coefficient by coefficient,
$Lf = \sum_k \lambda_k c_k\phi_k$. A coupled problem thus splits into many
small, independent ones. This is the reason spherical harmonics are used
horizontally (see [below](#spherical-harmonics-diagonalize-the-laplacian)).

The second is **fixed-point (Picard) iteration**. An equation of the form
$x = F(x)$ is solved by repeating $x_{k+1} = F(x_k)$ from a first guess. The
sequence converges when $F$ is a contraction, and it needs only evaluations
of $F$, not its Jacobian. The sea-level equation and its coupling to rotation
and to the viscoelastic memory are all solved this way.

Several terms carry the names of their originators. The dimensionless response
coefficients of a self-gravitating sphere are named after A. E. H. Love, who
introduced them in *Some Problems of Geodynamics* (1911). The horizontal
displacement number was added by T. Shida in 1912. The spring-and-damper
rheology of the mantle is named after J. C. Maxwell, who proposed it in 1867.
The sea-level equation in its modern form goes back to @FarrellClark1976.

## The mantle as a Maxwell body

On the timescales of glacial cycles the mantle behaves as both a solid and a
fluid. It responds elastically to a sudden change in load and flows viscously
under a load that persists. A **Maxwell body**, an elastic spring and a viscous
damper in series, captures both regimes with one constitutive law. For the
deviatoric stress $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ and strain $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ it
reads

$$
\dot{\boldsymbol{\tau}} + \frac{\mu}{\eta}\,\boldsymbol{\tau}
\;=\; 2\mu\,\dot{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}},
$$

where $\mu$ is the shear modulus and $\eta$ the viscosity. Under a suddenly
imposed strain the stress jumps to its elastic value and then decays on the
**Maxwell time**

$$
\tau_M \;=\; \frac{\eta}{\mu}.
$$

For the upper mantle of the benchmark earth model M3–L70–V01
($\eta = 10^{21}$ Pa s, $\mu \approx 7\times10^{10}$ Pa), $\tau_M$ is about
450 yr. A load that changes faster than this sees a largely elastic mantle,
while a load held for many Maxwell times sees a fluid one. Glacial cycles span
both regimes, so both must be represented in the same simulation.

The real mantle is not a single Maxwell body. It is a stack of layers, each
with its own density, shear modulus and viscosity, beneath an elastic
lithosphere and above a fluid core. The relaxation of the surface is therefore
not set by one Maxwell time. It is set by the whole structure, including the
buoyancy of the displaced material, and it typically spans hundreds to many
thousands of years. Viscosity may also vary laterally, for example between
cratons and tectonically active regions. This lateral structure is the main
reason a time-domain method was chosen for VILMA2.

::: {.callout-tip title="In VILMA2"}
The layered structure is built in `vilma_earth_structure` and selected by
`earth`: `"M3-L70-V01"` (default), `"PREM"` (density and shear modulus from
incompressible PREM on a given layer geometry) or `"custom"` (the layer arrays
`r_bot`, `r_top`, `rho`, `mu`, `eta`, `rheology`). An elastic layer
(`rheology = 0`) is exactly elastic, and a fluid layer (`rheology = 2`) carries
no shear stress. Lateral viscosity is off by default (`l_visc_3d = .false.`).
When it is on, a $\log_{10}\eta$ field is read from `visc_3d_file`, by default
the @Bagge2021 field of the FesmData store, and clamped to
`visc_log10_min`–`visc_log10_max` (19.5 to 30). The model does not ship a
viscosity file. See [Rheology](physics/rheology.qmd), and
[the 3-D viscosity input chain](physics/rheology.qmd#visc3d-input) for the
order in which the field is built.
:::

## Spherical harmonics diagonalize the Laplacian

Spherical harmonics are the natural basis for fields on a sphere. Any
square-integrable field on the surface can be expanded as

$$
f(\theta,\phi) \;=\; \sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell} f_{\ell m}\,Y_{\ell m}(\theta,\phi),
$$

where the degree $\ell$ sets the angular scale of a pattern and the order $m$
distributes its nodal lines between latitude and longitude. Zonal harmonics
($m = 0$) vary only with latitude, while sectoral harmonics ($|m| = \ell$) vary
only with longitude.

The use of this basis follows from one property. The spherical harmonics are
the eigenfunctions of the angular part of the Laplacian,

$$
\nabla_1^2\,Y_{\ell m} \;=\; -\,\ell(\ell+1)\,Y_{\ell m}.
$$

The Laplacian is thus diagonal in this basis, as described above. For a
radially symmetric Earth the field equations of a loaded, self-gravitating
sphere (momentum balance, Poisson's equation and incompressibility) decouple
degree by degree. Each degree $\ell$ reduces to an independent radial problem,
and the order $m$ enters only through the load coefficients. The operator of
a degree is therefore the same for all its orders.

In practice the expansion is truncated at a maximum degree $\ell_\max$. The
shortest resolved half-wavelength is about $\pi a/\ell_\max$, where $a$ is the
radius of the Earth. This gives roughly 310 km at $\ell_\max = 64$ and 120 km
at $\ell_\max = 170$, the resolution of VILMA1 in CLIMBER-X. The number of
coefficients grows as $(\ell_\max+1)^2$, so the cost rises steeply with
resolution.

::: {.callout-tip title="In VILMA2"}
`vilma_sht` wraps the SHTns library [@Schaeffer2013] and FFTW for the
transforms between the Gauss–Legendre grid and spectral space. The harmonics
are real and fully normalized, without the Condon–Shortley phase. The
truncation is set by `lmax` (64 in `input/vilma_defaults.nml`, while a host must
set it itself), and the grid by `nlat` and `nphi` (0 gives the de-aliased defaults
$2\ell_\max+2$ and $4\ell_\max$). SHTns is initialized without its per-grid
algorithm tuning. This is fixed in `vilma_sht` at compile time and is not a
run-time option. See [Spectral reduction](discretization/spectral.qmd) and
[Radial finite elements](discretization/radial-fe.qmd).
:::

## Load Love numbers, one response per degree

For a radially symmetric Earth the response to a surface load depends only on
the degree of the load, not on its order. A load coefficient $\sigma_{\ell m}$
therefore produces a vertical displacement, a horizontal displacement and a
perturbation of the gravitational potential that are fixed multiples of it.
These multiples are the **load Love numbers** $h_\ell$, $l_\ell$ and $k_\ell$,
respectively. Following @Farrell1972 they are defined relative to the
potential of the load itself, $\varphi^L = 4\pi G a\,\sigma/(2\ell+1)$:

$$
h_\ell = \frac{g_0\,U(a)}{\varphi^{L}}, \qquad
l_\ell = \frac{g_0\,V(a)}{\varphi^{L}}, \qquad
k_\ell = -\frac{F(a)}{\varphi^{L}} - 1,
$$

where $U(a)$ and $V(a)$ are the radial and horizontal displacement at the
surface, $F(a)$ is the incremental potential there and $g_0$ is surface
gravity. The term $-1$ in $k_\ell$ removes the direct potential of the load, so
that $k_\ell$ describes only the deformation.

For a viscoelastic Earth the Love numbers become functions of time. A load
applied at $t = 0$ produces an instantaneous elastic response, which then
relaxes toward the fluid limit as the mantle flows. For a homogeneous fluid
sphere this limit is known exactly, $h_\ell \to -(2\ell+1)/3$ and
$k_\ell \to -1$, which makes it a useful test of any GIA code.

Classical normal-mode codes write this time dependence as an elastic term
plus a finite sum of exponentially decaying modes [@Peltier1974]. The modes
are found once per degree, and the response to an arbitrary load history then
follows by convolution. This is efficient for a radially symmetric Earth.
However, it cannot represent lateral viscosity, which couples the degrees and
removes the per-degree response on which the method rests.

VILMA2 therefore does not compute modes. It solves the radial problem of each
degree directly in time, following @Martinec2000, so the Love numbers are not
inputs to the model. They are diagnostics that emerge from it: the first step
gives the elastic response, and a load held long enough gives the fluid limit.
The same per-degree solve then serves the 1-D and the 3-D case.

::: {.callout-tip title="In VILMA2"}
The radial problem of each degree is discretized with finite elements in
`vilma_radial_fe`, which also holds the Love-number extraction
(`loading_love`, `tidal_love`). The operator of each degree is factored once
by the banded solver in `vilma_band` and reused at every step. `vilma_response`
wraps the per-degree solves as a response operator, selected by
`earth_response`: `"ve"` (viscoelastic, default), `"elastic"` or `"null"`. The
elastic $h_\ell$ of M3–L70–V01 matches the reference table to within 0.08 % up
to degree 256 (see [Love numbers](benchmarks/love-numbers.qmd)).
:::

## The sea-level equation and its fingerprint

Sea-level change caused by a melting ice sheet is not uniform. The meltwater
raises the global mean, but the loss of ice mass also lowers the geoid near the
ice sheet and lets the bed rebound there. Relative sea level therefore falls
near a shrinking ice sheet and rises by more than the mean far from it. This
spatial pattern is the sea-level **fingerprint** of the ice sheet.

The **sea-level equation** computes this pattern self-consistently. With the
ocean function $C$ (1 over ocean, 0 over land and grounded ice), the
relative sea-level change $S$ is

$$
S \;=\; C\cdot\bigl(N - u + \Delta\phi\bigr),
$$

where $N$ is the geoid change, $u$ the vertical displacement of the bed and
$\Delta\phi$ a spatially uniform term. The Earth responds to the total surface
load,

$$
L \;=\; \rho_{\text{ice}}\,\Delta I \;+\; \rho_{\text{water}}\,C\cdot S,
$$

with $\Delta I$ the change in grounded ice thickness. The uniform term
$\Delta\phi$ is chosen such that the ocean gains exactly the mass the ice
loses. Since $S$ appears in its own load, the equation is implicit. It is
solved by fixed-point iteration: a guess of $S$ gives the load, the load gives
$N$ and $u$, and these give an updated $S$.

Two refinements matter for realistic geometries. First, the coastline
migrates. As sea level changes, land floods or emerges and grounded ice may
float, so the ocean function itself must be updated. Second, a newly flooded
cell does not fill instantly to the full sea-level change, and loading it as
if it did puts a spurious step at the shoreline. The first refinement follows
@KMM2005, and the second follows @Martinec2018.

::: {.callout-tip title="In VILMA2"}
`vilma_sle` solves the equation in the pseudo-spectral form of @KMM2005: the
response is applied in spectral space, and the product with the ocean function
is formed on the grid. An inner loop iterates $S$ at a fixed coastline
(`sle_n_inner` = 20, `sle_tol` = $10^{-7}$), and an outer loop migrates the
coastline (`sle_n_outer` = 3). The coastline migrates by default
(`sle_fixed_ocean = .false.`), and newly flooded cells are loaded by their
actual water column (`sle_subgrid = .true.`). Ocean mass is conserved by
construction. The densities default to `rho_ice` = 917 and `rho_water` =
1000 kg m$^{-3}$. Against the @Martinec2018 cases D3, E2 and F1 the model
agrees to within about 8 % of peak in every field. Case C2 shows an offset that
is not yet attributed. See [Sea-level equation](physics/sea-level.qmd) and its
[benchmark](benchmarks/sea-level.qmd).
:::

## Off-axis mass drives the rotation pole

A redistribution of surface mass changes the inertia tensor of the Earth and
thereby moves its rotation axis. Mass placed away from the poles and the
equator perturbs the off-diagonal products of inertia, and the pole drifts in
response. This **true polar wander** changes the centrifugal potential, which
acts as a further load on the Earth and on the ocean. This feedback has no
global mean. Instead, it shifts sea level in a characteristic degree-2,
order-1 pattern.

On GIA timescales the Chandler wobble can be neglected. The polar motion
$\mathbf{m}$ then follows the quasi-static linearized Liouville equation
[@MartinecHagedoorn2014],

$$
\Bigl[\,1 - \tfrac{k^{T}(t)}{k_{s}}\,\Bigr] * \mathbf{m}(t) \;=\; \frac{I(t)}{C-A},
$$

where $*$ is a convolution in time, $I$ is the inertia perturbation including
the deformation of the Earth, $k^T$ is the degree-2 tidal Love number, $k_s$
the secular (fluid-limit) Love number and $C-A$ the difference between the
polar and equatorial moments of inertia. The centrifugal potential of the
displaced pole,

$$
\Lambda \;=\; -\Omega^{2}a^{2}\sin\theta\cos\theta\,(m_1\cos\phi + m_2\sin\phi),
$$

is a degree-2, order-1 field. It enters the sea-level equation as one more
contribution to the sea surface, so no separate solver is needed.

::: {.callout-tip title="In VILMA2"}
`vilma_rotation` carries two degree-2 viscoelastic channels (one forced by the
load, one by the centrifugal potential) on the same radial operator as the load
response. The rotation and the sea level are iterated to a common fixed point
inside `vilma_sle`. Rotation is on by default (`rotation = .true.`) and is
switched off for the non-rotating community benchmarks. `rotation_k_s` = 0
(default) uses the model's own fluid limit for $k_s$, and `rotation_c_minus_a`
sets $C-A$ (default $2.63\times10^{35}$ kg m$^2$). The polar motion matches
Spada test 3/2 to within 0.9 %. See [Rotation](physics/rotation.qmd) and its
[benchmark](benchmarks/rotation.qmd).
:::

## Explicit memory and time stepping

VILMA2 advances the Maxwell rheology explicitly in time. The total stress at a
step is the elastic stress of the current strain plus a **memory stress**
$\boldsymbol{\tau}^V$ that carries the relaxation history. In the default
scheme it is updated as

$$
\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V,i} \;=\; (1-M)\,\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V,i-1}
\;-\; 2\mu M\,\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{\,i},
\qquad
M \;=\; \frac{\mu\,\Delta t}{\eta},
$$

where $i$ is the step index and $M$ is the Maxwell number of the step
[@Martinec2000]. The memory stress enters only the right-hand side of the field
equations. The left-hand operator is therefore independent of time, of the
time step and of viscosity. It is factored once per degree, and each step
costs a back-substitution.

This choice has two consequences. First, lateral viscosity changes only the
scalar $M$, which multiplies known fields pointwise. The memory advance is
then done on the grid and transformed back to spectral space, while the solve
stays decoupled by degree. Second, the scheme is only conditionally stable.
The step must satisfy $\Delta t < 2\eta_{\min}/\mu$, so the lowest viscosity
present sets the step. At the default floor of $10^{19.5}$ Pa s and
$\mu \approx 7\times10^{10}$ Pa the limit $M \le 1$ is about 15 yr. The
coupling interval of a host model is thus split into shorter sub-steps, with
the ice load interpolated linearly across the interval.

A second, implicit scheme is available. The trapezoidal (Crank–Nicolson)
update is second-order accurate and A-stable, so its step is limited by
accuracy rather than stability. Its step size is chosen adaptively, by
comparing one full step with two half steps. Since the end-of-step strain
depends on the end-of-step memory, each step is iterated together with the
sea-level equation.

::: {.callout-tip title="In VILMA2"}
The memory scheme is selected by `scheme`: `"fe"` (explicit, default), with
equal sub-steps at $M \le$ `cfl` (default 1), or `"trap"` (trapezoidal,
adaptive), with the tolerances `rtol` = $10^{-4}$ and `atol` = $10^{-3}$. The
sub-step controller is `vilma_timestep`, the per-degree Maxwell kernel is in
`vilma_viscoelastic`, and the field driver is in `vilma_response`. A host
advances the model with `solid_earth_update(se, h_ice, dt_yr)` from
`vilma_coupling`, which passes the coupling interval in years. With lateral
viscosity the toroidal field is carried by default (`l_toroidal = .true.`).
A deglaciation at $\ell_\max = 170$ with 3-D viscosity then takes about
2.7 min of wall time per kyr on 64 threads (see
[Toroidal flow](physics/toroidal.qmd)). A restarted run reproduces an
uninterrupted one bit for bit. See [Rheology](physics/rheology.qmd#memory-time-schemes)
and [Time stepping](discretization/time-stepping.qmd).
:::

## Where to go next

The [Install & run](getting-started.qmd) page describes how to build the
model, configure it through the `&vilma` and `&ctl` namelists and run the
standalone driver. Every `&vilma` parameter and its default is listed in
`input/vilma_defaults.nml`. The [Physics](physics/governing-equations.qmd) and

behind each section above, and the [Benchmarks](benchmarks/index.qmd) show how
well each part reproduces published reference solutions.
